questions.q: Name the four main materials used in traditional pankha making and state one property of each that makes it suitable for fan construction.
questions.a: Bamboo: light, flexible, strong — ideal for frames and handles. Cane: pliable when soaked, strong when dry — ideal for woven patterns. Palm leaf: wide, flat, stiff when dried — ideal for flat circular fans. Silk: lightweight, decorative, holds shape when stretched — ideal for decorative fans. A wrong answer (e.g., "plastic and metal") lists modern materials not discussed in the traditional craft context.

questions.q: Why is bamboo a common material for pankha frames in monsoon regions of India?
questions.a: Bamboo grows abundantly in monsoon regions, making it cheap and locally available. It is light (easy to hold), flexible (bends without breaking), and strong (does not snap under pressure). Green bamboo can be shaped; dry bamboo holds its shape. These properties make it ideal for pankha frames and handles. A wrong answer (e.g., "because it looks nice") focuses on aesthetics rather than the functional and geographic reasons for bamboo's use.

questions.q: Describe the technique of making a palm leaf pankha in three steps.
questions.a: Step 1: Harvest mature palm leaves and dry them flat to prevent curling. Step 2: Cut the dried leaf into a circular or semicircular shape. Step 3: Stitch the leaf to a bamboo or wooden handle, securing it with thread or thin cane. The result is a stiff, flat fan that creates a strong breeze. A wrong answer that omits drying (e.g., "just cut and attach") ignores that undried leaves will curl and become unusable.

questions.q: How does the technique for cane pankha differ from that for palm leaf pankha?
questions.a: Cane pankha requires soaking the cane in water to make it pliable, then weaving thin strips into a pattern — the technique is additive (building up a pattern from strips). Palm leaf pankha requires drying a whole leaf, cutting it to shape, and mounting it on a handle — the technique is subtractive (cutting from a single piece) and mounting. Cane weaving is time-intensive and requires skill in pattern-making; palm leaf mounting is simpler but requires careful drying. A wrong answer (e.g., "they are the same") ignores the fundamental difference between weaving and cutting/mounting techniques.

questions.q: Explain how regional geography determines the choice of pankha material. Give two examples.
questions.a: Geography determines material availability. Example 1: Coastal South India has abundant palm trees, so palm leaf pankhas are common there. Example 2: Northeast India has cane forests, so woven cane pankhas are a specialty of that region. Example 3: Mulberry-growing regions (Karnataka, Bengal) produce silk, so silk pankhas are associated with these regions. The material is not a matter of preference but of what grows locally. A wrong answer (e.g., "all regions use the same material") ignores the geographic basis of craft traditions.

questions.q: A craftsperson wants to make a decorative pankha for a wedding gift. Which material would you recommend and why? Consider aesthetics, cost, and cultural significance.
questions.a: Silk is the best choice for a decorative wedding pankha because: (1) Aesthetics — silk is smooth, colorful, and can be embroidered or painted with decorative designs. (2) Cultural significance — silk is associated with prosperity and celebration in Indian culture, making it appropriate for a wedding. (3) Cost — silk is more expensive than bamboo or palm leaf, but for a special occasion gift, the cost is justified. Bamboo or palm leaf would be more practical for everyday use but less suitable for a decorative gift. A wrong answer (e.g., "bamboo because it is cheap") ignores the decorative and cultural requirements of a wedding gift.
